title: I ran claude plugin eval on 89 skills. The trigger rate fell from 100% to 55.6%.
summary: Claude Code shipped a plugin eval tool that tests skill triggers by running test cases in isolation and comparing results with/without the plugin loaded. The author tested 89 existing skills and found only a 55.6% trigger rate, revealing many skills silently fail to get invoked without any error signal. This tool enables developers to measure actual plugin impact rather than rely on guesswork.
content:
The problem with skills is that failure is silent


My coffee e-commerce project has 89 skill directories under it. Each one exists because I got burned: remember the GRANT on that migration, keep those three layers in sync when you rename a column, query the database before you guess at the code.
Skills work by having the model read their descriptions and decide, on its own, whether to invoke one. That's the whole problem. When it doesn't invoke, nothing happens. No error, no warning, no log line. You just watch the AI start working, and find out two days later that it skipped the rule.
I measured this by hand once, back in July: four natural-language prompts, four sessions, counting how many times the skill name showed up in the reply. Sonnet hit 3 of 4, Haiku hit 1 of 4. I wrote the numbers into my project rules and never measured again, because doing it by hand is expensive and gives you a one-off number that goes stale.
Last week Claude Code quietly shipped claude plugin eval.
You write test cases — realistic sentences a user might type — plus graders that score the result. Each case runs in a fresh isolated session, three times by default because the model is non-deterministic.
Standard stuff. What surprised me: it runs a second arm by default, with your plugin not loaded at all.
The difference between the two scores is Δ. The docs put it bluntly:
If a case scores 1.0 both with and without the plugin, the plugin isn't what made it pass.
Vendors don't usually ship a default that proves their users' work is useless. This design concedes something: your skill might be doing nothing, and you'd have no way to know.
I reused the four prompts from July rather than writing new ones. Writing your own test corpus has a trap — you unconsciously write sentences your skill happens to catch. The old corpus was written before I knew what I'd be measuring.

title: Music Royalties Tokenization in Brazil: Monetize Your Work with Blockchain
summary: Brazil's music industry faces delays in royalty payments to artists due to multiple intermediaries, with independent musicians waiting 6-9 months to receive payment for tracks. The author proposes blockchain tokenization on Stellar network as a solution, allowing automatic micropayment distribution through smart contracts with fractions-of-a-cent transaction costs. This approach could reduce payment delays and increase transparency for music creators.
content:
Every time a song plays on the radio, streams on Spotify, or soundtracks a viral video, money changes hands. Yet for most Brazilian artists, that money arrives late, fragmented, and shrouded in opacity. Having spent two decades building blockchain infrastructure, I've watched tokenization evolve from a buzzword into a genuine solution for one of the music industry's oldest problems: how creators actually get paid.
Brazil's music market is massive. According to Pró-Música Brasil, streaming revenue surpassed R$3 billion in 2023, with the country ranking among the world's top ten music markets. But the distribution pipeline remains inefficient. Royalties pass through collecting societies like ECAD, publishers, labels, and distributors—each layer adding delay and cost.
An independent artist in Recife might wait six to nine months to receive payment for a track, often without clear visibility into how the figure was calculated. The problem isn't a lack of money; it's a lack of transparency and speed in moving it. When I analyze these systems from a digital forensics perspective, the recurring issue is the same: no single source of truth. Every intermediary keeps its own ledger, and reconciling them is where value and time evaporate.
Tokenizing music royalties means representing the future revenue rights of a song as digital assets on a blockchain. On networks like Stellar, this becomes practical rather than theoretical. Stellar's low transaction costs—fractions of a cent—make it viable to distribute micropayments to thousands of rights holders automatically.
Here's the concrete mechanism I've helped design in projects: a smart contract, built with Soroban, holds the royalty distribution logic. When streaming revenue enters the contract, it splits automatically according to predefined percentages—say, 50% to the artist, 20% to the producer, 15% to the songwriter, and 15% to token holders who invested in the work.

title: Wazuh loses events three ways under load, and only one of them raises an alert

The analysis reveals that buffer overflow cases can drop significant numbers of security events with minimal or no monitoring alerts. This highlights critical gaps in Wazuh's default alerting for event loss.

title: Mastering GitHub Codespaces Storage: A Guide for Productivity and Cost Control
summary: GitHub Codespaces bills storage based on allocated disk capacity (32 GB by default) rather than actual file usage, and stopped instances continue consuming storage charges. Students hit free tier storage limits despite minimal codebase sizes, illustrating the gap between perceived and actual infrastructure costs. Understanding provisioned capacity billing is critical for managing Codespaces expenses.
content:
In the fast-paced world of software development, cloud-based developer environments like GitHub Codespaces have become indispensable. They promise instant setup, consistent environments, and enhanced collaboration, boosting developer productivity. Yet, as a recent GitHub Community discussion illuminated, the path to seamless productivity can be fraught with unexpected challenges—specifically, managing storage usage and avoiding hidden costs.
Computer Science teacher Jim McCormick sparked the conversation, highlighting a common pain point for educators and developers alike: students hitting GitHub Codespaces free tier storage limits despite seemingly minimal actual file usage. This scenario, common in environments utilizing modern software engineering management tools, underscores a critical need for clarity in cloud resource billing and proactive management.
Jim's initial confusion stemmed from GitHub reporting usage as "15 GB-hr" while free accounts offer "15 GB-month." He correctly pointed out that "15 GB-hr" would imply an incredibly small allowance, especially when his students' actual codebases were under 2GB. This apparent discrepancy, and the rapid exhaustion of free limits, left him and his students in a bind.
The core of the problem, as clarified by community experts, lies in how GitHub Codespaces provisions and meters disk storage. It's not about the size of your repository alone; it's about the allocated infrastructure.
- **Default Provisioned Disk Size:** Even if a student's repository or code takes up only a few hundred megabytes or a couple of gigabytes, GitHub Codespaces by default provisions a **32 GB block storage disk** for standard virtual machines. Crucially, storage usage is calculated based on this *allocated disk capacity*, not merely the amount of space currently occupied by files inside the container.

title: I Built a Journal That Doesn't Spy on You
summary: JournalMind is a journaling app that runs AI inference locally on-device rather than sending data to remote servers, eliminating privacy concerns that inhibit authentic journaling. The author argues that modern hardware makes client-side AI powerful enough to replace cloud processing for many use cases. This shift removes the "observer effect" where users self-censor knowing their data will be processed remotely.
content:
We’ve all been there: you type out a deeply personal thought, hit save, and then a tiny voice in the back of your head whispers, “Wait, where did that data go?”
For years, I’ve been a skeptic of cloud-based journaling apps. The promise of AI-driven insights is seductive, but the trade-off—sending your most intimate secrets to a remote server to be processed by a third-party model—felt like too high a price for privacy. So, I decided to build JournalMind not as another SaaS product, but as a proof-of-concept for what’s possible when we stop treating user data as fuel for the AI engine and start treating it as sacred.
The biggest misconception in the current AI wave is that intelligence requires the cloud. We’ve been conditioned to believe that if an app is smart, it must be talking to a massive data center somewhere in Virginia or Oregon. But the hardware in our pockets and on our desks has quietly become powerful enough to change that narrative.
JournalMind is built on a simple premise: your thoughts stay on your device. Every word you type, every mood tag you select, and every insight generated is processed locally in your browser using a private on-device AI. Nothing is sent to our servers for analysis. Not even metadata.
Why does this matter? Because privacy isn’t just about compliance; it’s about psychological safety. When I was building the core logic, I realized that the fear of being "watched" changes how people write. You hesitate. You self-censor. You don’t write the raw, ugly, beautiful truth because you imagine a machine—or worse, a human auditor—might eventually see it. By moving the AI inference layer to the client side, we remove that observer effect. You can write as if you’re the only person in the room, because technically, you are.
Building this wasn’t just about slapping a “Privacy First” badge on the landing page. It required a complete rethink of the architecture. Traditional SaaS apps rely on the server to do the heavy lifting. In JournalMind,

zh.title: 我建造了一个不监视你的日记应用

title: I vibe-coded a mission control for my coding agents — and now I use it every day
summary: termist is a terminal UI and daemon for managing multiple concurrent Claude Code and other coding agent sessions across projects, providing a unified view of agent status and enabling follow-up prompts without terminal switching. The tool was built through "vibe coding" using Claude Code itself to build a tool for managing Claude Code. The project highlights that code generation accelerates scaffolding but does not eliminate difficult architectural decisions.
content:
I run coding agents every day. Usually more than one at a time.
Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode are all useful on their own, but the workflow gets messy quickly: one agent is running, another is waiting for permission, a third has finished, and all of them are sitting in different terminal tabs.
After a while, the hard question is not “how do I start another agent?” It is:
Which agent is waiting for me right now?
That question became the reason I built termist.
termist is a local terminal UI and background daemon for running coding-agent sessions across projects and worktrees.

Every session appears as a card with a status dot. I can see which agents are running, which ones need input, which ones are done, and which ones can be resumed after a restart. A single key takes me to the next session that needs attention.
It also lets me send a follow-up prompt without opening the session's terminal pane. When I close the TUI, the daemon keeps the sessions alive. When the machine restarts, the sessions come back and can be resumed.
The goal is not to replace a terminal emulator, an editor or Git. It is a small control layer for the agent-heavy part of my workflow.
The entire project was built through a vibe-coding workflow. I used Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode heavily while designing, implementing, testing and iterating on termist.
That made the project unusually self-referential. I was using coding agents to build a tool for managing coding agents, then using the tool to run more coding agents.
Vibe coding was useful for getting from an idea to a working product quickly. It helped with scaffolding, repetitive code, experiments and UI iterations. But it did not remove the difficult parts.
The difficult parts were deciding what the product should actually do, checking whether the status model matched reality, dealing with process lifetimes, testing cancellation and restart behavior, and manually trying the real CLI tools in a real terminal.

title: I'd rather not ask
summary: A translation layer abstracts a row of inconsistent translation engines (different error handling, response formats, and result ordering) behind a single clean interface, shielding callers from complexity. The real work is handling partial failures—batches that translate some segments while failing on others—while billing accurately only for completed work. The maintainer intentionally hides underlying inconsistencies to create a simpler contract than the messy reality.
content:
From the outside, the translation layer I maintain has one interface. You hand it a set of segments. For each segment you get back one of two things: a translation, or an error code. That is the whole contract. It looks calm.
It is not calm. The calm is something I make.
Behind that interface is a row of engines, and no two of them agree on anything. One returns HTTP 200 for its own failures and hides the real status as an integer in the body. One answers in JSON until the input gets large and then switches to XML. One returns its results as two unordered lists you reconcile by id. One has a job state that runs backwards. One isn't on the network at all — it's a native library in my own process that, on a bad day, becomes a zombie in the process table and never returns.
Not one of them produces the shape my interface promises. The single result-or-error the caller sees does not exist out there. I assemble it.
So the contract isn't something I found by reading documentation. It's something I manufacture, at the boundary, one engine at a time. Every lie gets caught and rewritten into the one vocabulary the caller speaks. The 200 that means failure becomes an error code. The two lists become per-segment results, matched by id. The zombie becomes a clean "this didn't finish." The caller never learns any of it. They asked for translations; they get translations, or honest errors, in the order they expect. They stay naive because I decided they would.
The easy version of this is the engine that wholly succeeds or wholly fails. The real work is the middle: the batch that translated forty segments, errored on three, and then dropped the connection. The engine that returned results and a charge for work it never finished.
An honest interface has to be granular about that. This segment succeeded. This one carries an error. And — the part I care about most — you do not bill for what didn't come back. If a segment was skipped, it's skipped. If the engine billed me for work that

zh.title: 我宁可不问
zh.summary: 翻译层将一行不一致的翻译引擎（不同的错误处理、响应格式和结果排序）抽象为单个清晰的接口，保护调用者免受复杂性的影响。真正的工作是处理部分故障——那些翻译某些片段而其他片段失败的批次——同时只对已完成的工作准确计费。维护者故意隐藏底层的不一致性，以创建比混乱现实更简洁的契约。

title: Traffic from ChatGPT now brings a quarter of our sign-ups. How we track it, and what we changed
summary: A Japanese freelance marketplace saw ChatGPT referrals grow from 3.7% of sign-ups in April to 24.5% by September, far exceeding other AI tools combined. The author discovered critical tracking issues: ChatGPT links were mislabeled as Twitter traffic due to link shortener overlap, and most ChatGPT traffic lacks referrer headers but includes utm_source in landing URLs. Analyzing landing URLs rather than referrer headers revealed the true traffic source.
content:
My Website is a freelance marketplace in Japan that I've run since 2004.
Over the last few weeks, more and more of the people signing up have been arriving from ChatGPT.





Month
Share of sign-ups from ChatGPT




April
3.7%


May
10.6%


June
14.5%


July
15.3%


August
13.3%


September (1st to 26th)
24.5%



In the week of September 21 (six days so far), it was 33%. One in three.
Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot and Claude together were 1.4% of sign-ups over the whole period, against 14.6% for ChatGPT. Almost all of it is ChatGPT.
The counting turned out to be the hard part.
Since April 4, the site has recorded where each member first arrived from. On the first visit it stores the referrer and the landing URL in a cookie, keeps them for 30 days, and writes them to the member's record when they sign up.
Two things went wrong with that.
1. ChatGPT was being counted as X.
chatgpt.com contains the string t.co, which is X's link shortener. So ChatGPT visits were labeled as coming from X. I fixed that on April 18.
2. Most ChatGPT visits have no referrer at all.
?utm_source=chatgpt.com on the landing URL, which ChatGPT adds to the links it shows. Our admin screen was deciding the source from the referrer only, so those sign-ups all showed up as "unknown". On August 24 I changed it to check the landing URL's utm_source first.
The landing URL itself had been saved all along, so every number in this post is recounted from the raw records, not from what the admin screen used to show.
If you're checking your own site, look at the landing URL, not only the referrer.

summary: Introduces wFabricSecurity's token-bucket rate limiting for Hyperledger Fabric endorsement nodes, protecting against CPU exhaustion from unthrottled ECDSA signature verification requests.
content:
Defiende tus nodos de endoso: Rate limiting token-bucket para Fabric.



Día 07 de la serie técnica wFabricSecurity Open Source.
Verificar firmas ECDSA es costoso en CPU. Saturar un peer de endoso tumbará el nodo. wFabricSecurity defiende tu clúster con rate limiting token-bucket.

Agotamiento de CPU en nodos criptográficos al verificar firmas ECDSA sin límite

from wFabricSecurity.security import RateLimiter
from wFabricSecurity.core import RateLimitError

# Configure limiter: max 100 tokens, refills at 10 tokens/sec
limiter = RateLimiter(capacity=100, refill_rate=10.0)

try:
    if limiter.consume(participant="CN=WorkerNode_01", tokens=1):
        process_endorsement_request()
except RateLimitError:
    # Protects expensive ECDSA verification from overload
    print("RATE LIMIT EXCEEDED: Back off and retry later.")

Límites por Participante: Aplica cuotas diferentes por Common Name (CN) o dirección IP.
Control RateLimitError: Rechaza picos abusivos antes de consumir CPU en criptografía.

title: Seguridad no bloqueante: Gestión asíncrona de secretos con asyncio.
summary: Guide to wauth's async_set, async_get, and async_valid methods for non-blocking secret management in FastAPI, preventing event loop freezing during cryptographic operations.
content:
Seguridad no bloqueante: Gestión asíncrona de secretos con asyncio.


Las llamadas síncronas de base de datos y criptografía son los asesinos silenciosos de la concurrencia en FastAPI. wauth ofrece async_set, async_get y async_valid nativos para mantener tu event loop al máximo.
Esta es la implementación exacta para producción de Asynchronous API (async_set, async_get, async_valid):
import asyncio
from wauth import WAuth

auth = WAuth()

async def authenticate_request(api_key: str) -> bool:
    # Non-blocking, constant-time verification in async coroutine
    is_valid = await auth.async_valid("SERVICE_API_KEY", api_key)
    return is_valid

async def main():
    await auth.async_set("SERVICE_API_KEY", "sk_live_994821")
    authorized = await authenticate_request("sk_live_994821")
    print(f"Request authorized: {authorized}")

asyncio.run(main())

Métodos Async Nativos: async_set(), async_get(), async_delete() y async_valid().
Optimizado para FastAPI: Inyéctalo directo en dependencias de rutas async sin congelar el bucle.
Cálculo Offloaded: Las operaciones criptográficas se delegan de forma segura sin bloquear I/O.
Consultas y operaciones criptográficas síncronas que bloquean el event loop en microservicios async
Latencia en endpoints de FastAPI que validan claves de API de usuarios con frecuencia
Cuellos de botella de concurrencia cuando cientos de corrutinas consultan secretos a la vez

pip install wauth

title: Estimación de cardinalidad hiper-eficiente: Redis HyperLogLog en producción con wredis
summary: Covers wredis's RedisHLLManager for hyper-efficient cardinality estimation, enabling counting of millions of unique elements using only ~12 KB memory per counter with <0.81% error.
content:
Estimación de cardinalidad hiper-eficiente: Redis HyperLogLog en producción con wredis


Contar elementos únicos en millones de usuarios activos diarios, direcciones IP o eventos telemétricos IoT en una base de datos relacional tradicional o en un Set estándar de Redis agota rápidamente la memoria RAM disponible.
Un Set en Redis almacenando 100 millones de UUIDs requiere varios gigabytes de RAM. En contraste, Redis HyperLogLog (HLL) implementa un algoritmo de estimación probabilística que acota el consumo de memoria a una cantidad constante de ~12 KB por clave, manteniendo un error estándar inferior al 0.81%.
wredis?


Con wredis, las operaciones de cardinalidad se integran con tipado estricto, gestión automática del ciclo de vida TTL y pooling de conexiones de alta concurrencia:
from wredis import RedisHLLManager

# Inicialización del gestor HLL con pooling empresarial
hll_manager = RedisHLLManager(host="localhost", port=6379, db=0)

# Registro de visitantes únicos diarios distribuidos
clave_visitantes_hoy = "visitantes:2026-09-20"

# Ingesta masiva de identificadores únicos con latencia sub-milisegundo
lote_usuarios_1 = [f"usuario_{i}" for i in range(100000)]
hll_manager.add(clave_visitantes_hoy, *lote_usuarios_1, ttl=86400)

lote_usuarios_2 = [f"usuario_{i}" for i in range(50000, 150000)]
hll_manager.add(clave_visitantes_hoy, *lote_usuarios_2)

# Estimación de cardinalidad total única con memoria acotada (~12 KB)
total_unicos = hll_manager.count(clave_visitantes_hoy)
print(f"Visitantes únicos estimados: {total_unicos}")
# Resultado esperado ~150,000 registros únicos con <0.81% de margen de error

Huella de memoria constante: Exactamente 12 KB por contador, ya sea rastreando 10.000 o 10.000.000 de registros distintos.
Fusión ultrarrápida (Merge): Unifica múltiples claves HyperLogLog (e.g., métricas diarias en acumulados semanales o mensuales) directamente en el servidor Redis sin transferir datos masivos a la aplicación.
TTL nativo y control de ciclo de vida: Evit

title: Hyper-efficient Cardinality Estimation: Redis HyperLogLog in Production with wredis
summary: Details how Redis HyperLogLog with wredis enables efficient unique element counting across millions of records using constant ~12 KB memory while maintaining sub-1% error rates.
content:
Hyper-efficient Cardinality Estimation: Redis HyperLogLog in Production with wredis


Counting unique elements across millions of daily active users, IP addresses, or IoT telemetry events in a traditional relational database or standard Redis Set quickly consumes gigabytes of memory. 
A Redis Set storing 100 million UUIDs requires several gigabytes of RAM. In contrast, Redis HyperLogLog (HLL) uses a probabilistic counting algorithm that bounds memory consumption to a constant ~12 KB per key, maintaining a standard error of less than 0.81%.
wredis?


With wredis, cardinality operations are integrated seamlessly with type safety and automatic TTL management:
from wredis import RedisHLLManager

# Initialize HLL manager with enterprise connection pooling
hll_manager = RedisHLLManager(host="localhost", port=6379, db=0)

# Track unique daily visitors across distributed nodes
daily_visitors_key = "visitors:2026-09-20"

# Add batches of unique IDs with sub-millisecond overhead
user_batch_1 = [f"user_{i}" for i in range(100000)]
hll_manager.add(daily_visitors_key, *user_batch_1, ttl=86400)

user_batch_2 = [f"user_{i}" for i in range(50000, 150000)]
hll_manager.add(daily_visitors_key, *user_batch_2)

# Estimate total unique cardinality with bounded memory (~12 KB)
cardinality = hll_manager.count(daily_visitors_key)
print(f"Estimated unique visitors: {cardinality}")
# Expected ~150,000 unique records with <0.81% standard error

Constant Memory Footprint: Exactly 12 KB per counter, whether tracking 10,000 or 10,000,000 distinct items.
Fast Merging: Merge multiple HyperLogLog keys (e.g., daily metrics into weekly/monthly aggregates) without pulling raw records back to the application server.
Automatic TTL Lifecycle: Protect clusters against uncollected analytical debris.

title: AI Made Me Write Less Code — and Think More About Engineering
summary: Reflection on building a full-stack application using AI assistance while maintaining engineering control through spec-driven development, prioritizing architecture and design decisions.
content:
What I learned building and deploying a full-stack application with AI-assisted development, from the first specification to HTTPS on a GCP VM.
I had been tracking my workouts in Google Sheets for quite some time.
It worked. But eventually I started thinking: why am I still maintaining a spreadsheet for something this simple?
I had wanted to build a small workout tracker for a while, but there was one thing holding me back: frontend development isn't my strongest area.
So I decided to turn the project into an experiment.
I wanted to see how far I could go with AI-assisted software development — but not through what is commonly called vibe coding, where you describe an idea, let the AI generate a lot of code, and iterate mostly by looking at the result.
Instead, I wanted to remain involved in the engineering decisions at every stage.
The result surprised me.
About 99% of the code in the application was written by AI.
But I didn't feel like I had outsourced the engineering.
If anything, I spent more time thinking about requirements, specifications, architecture, trade-offs, reviewing changes, testing, and deployment.
This is what that experience looked like.
I've experimented with vibe coding before.
It is incredibly impressive how quickly you can get something working.
But I also found myself feeling that the implementation was slowly moving out of my control.
The AI might decide:
how the application should be structured
how components should look
how state should be managed
how APIs should be designed
which libraries should be introduced
how different pieces should interact
And eventually, I would have an application that worked, but I wasn't necessarily confident that I understood how it got there.
I wanted to try something different.
At work, I had already been introduced to Spec-Driven Development (SDD). I hadn't yet had the opportunity to work with it deeply, so this project became a way to experiment with that approach myself.
My rough development loop became:

title: Feeding the OLAP beast: ClickHouse massive bulk ingestion steps.
summary: Explains optimal bulk ingestion strategies for ClickHouse using ClickHouseBulkStep to avoid performance degradation from row-by-row inserts, integrated with wpipe-steps pipeline framework.
content:
Feeding the OLAP beast: ClickHouse massive bulk ingestion steps.


ClickHouse is a columnar beast, but treating it like MySQL by inserting row-by-row will bring your cluster to its knees. ClickHouseBulkStep packages optimal bulk buffering into a reusable step.
Here is how you use ClickHouseBulkStep & OLAP Pipelines in a production pipeline with wpipe-steps:
from wpipe import Pipeline
from wpipe_steps.database import ClickHouseBulkStep

pipeline = Pipeline(pipeline_name="telemetry_ingest")

pipeline.set_steps([
    ClickHouseBulkStep.as_step(
        name="insert_telemetry_batch",
        host="clickhouse.production.internal",
        database="analytics",
        table="device_telemetry",
        data_key="telemetry_batch",
        response_key="clickhouse_status"
    )
])

sample_batch = [
    {"sensor_id": f"S-{i}", "temp": 24.5 + i, "timestamp": "2026-09-19 12:00:00"}
    for i in range(10000)
]

result = pipeline.run({"telemetry_batch": sample_batch})
print(f"Inserted {result['clickhouse_status']['count']} records successfully!")

196 cataloged steps covering Redis, ClickHouse, MySQL, WAF, S3, Docker, and local HuggingFace AI.
Lazy-loading imports for instant sub-100ms startup times.
Clean .as_step() factory interface.
